entities.name: Tomáš Štítný ze Štítného
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tomáš Štítný ze Štítného (c. 1330 – 1409) stands as a foundational figure in Czech literary and religious history, a nobleman from Štítné in southern Bohemia whose intellectual and spiritual endeavors profoundly shaped the pre-Hussite reform movement. Living through a period of burgeoning national identity and growing calls for ecclesiastical reform within the Holy Roman Empire, Štítný dedicated his life to making complex scholastic theology and Christian ethics accessible to the Czech laity, primarily through extensive writings in the vernacular. His work represents a pivotal shift from Latin-dominated discourse, establishing Czech as a viable language for sophisticated theological and philosophical expression and thereby anticipating the broader European Reformation by over a century.

Štítný's prolific output included original treatises and translations, most notably his *Knížky šestery o obecných věcech křesťanských* (Six Books on General Christian Matters), completed around 1376. This monumental work, alongside others like *Řeči besední* (Table Talks) and *Život svatého Jeronýma* (Life of Saint Jerome), synthesized Augustinian theology, Aristotelian philosophy, and contemporary scholastic thought into a practical guide for Christian living. Educated at the University of Prague, Štítný engaged with the intellectual currents of his time, yet consciously chose to disseminate knowledge not among the clergy or academics, but directly to the Czech-speaking noble and urban classes, employing a clear, didactic style that resonated deeply with a population eager for spiritual instruction.

entities.summary:
Tomáš Štítný ze Štítného (c. 1333–1409) emerged from the Bohemian nobility as a pivotal intellectual and spiritual figure, whose writings in the Czech vernacular profoundly shaped the religious and cultural landscape of Central Europe on the eve of the Hussite Wars. Educated at the nascent Charles University in Prague, Štítný was not merely a scholar but a fervent advocate for lay piety and Christian ethics, translating complex theological concepts into accessible prose for a broader audience. His work represents a crucial bridge between scholastic tradition and the burgeoning demands for church reform, establishing him as a foundational architect of Czech literary and spiritual identity.

Štítný's principal achievements include his extensive translations of Latin theological texts into Czech, notably parts of the Bible and works of the Church Fathers, and original treatises such as "Knížky šestery o obecných věcech křesťanských" (Six Books on General Christian Matters) and "Řeči besední" (Table Talks). Through these works, he championed moral living, the importance of individual spiritual understanding, and the right of the laity to engage directly with scripture, often drawing from Augustine and Bernard of Clairvaux. His innovative use of the Czech language demonstrated its capacity for sophisticated philosophical and theological discourse, enriching its vocabulary and solidifying its grammatical structures during a period when Latin dominated academic and religious spheres.
